account: Today I have kept my morning office hours, inspected the mill's grain stock at ten, and had lunch at home. I am now at town hall for the thirteen hundred council letters, with tea at the neighbour's dockside cottage at fifteen hundred still scheduled. Something unusual seems to be drawing the local tradespeople together. Several townsfolk have repeated reports of a bridge or port change discussed at the bakery, naming the baker, builder, innkeeper, freight and neighbour, but I have seen no proposal and these repeated rumours are not independent confirmation. The innkeeper says he is merely arranging bread supplies and has seen no proposal; the neighbour could not give me definite information. Yesterday I saw the builder give the baker planks and a lantern. Those could be for ordinary work, landing improvements, or preparations for an event; I do not know which. Freight has recommended lighting both ferry landings and marking safe waiting areas, which is a concrete public concern rather than proof of a hidden project. The clearest explanation for some of the coordination is tonight's approved civic presentation: the appointment supplement says the inn and local tradespeople will express appreciation of municipal public service in the great hall from eighteen hundred to eighteen thirty, and asks me not to arrive early because organisers need time to prepare. That might account for the materials and discreet conversations, perhaps a celebratory presentation, but I cannot yet connect them with certainty. The baker, neighbour, innkeeper and secretary are all near town hall now. I should keep my appointments and attend the presentation at exactly eighteen hundred, rather than treating uncertain market talk as established fact.
